Analyse a reference video: camera moves, pacing and suggestions
Stillness lets the performance carry the scene. The audience studies faces and details because nothing else moves.
Moving closer pulls the audience into the character’s head. It signals that this moment matters: a realisation, a decision, rising tension.
Backing away isolates the character and reveals the world around them. Often used for loneliness, defeat or an ending.
A zoom magnifies without changing perspective, so it feels more “noticed” than “felt”. Compare it with a push-in to see the difference in depth.
Sideways movement creates parallax: near objects pass faster than far ones, which makes a flat set feel deep and alive.
Changing height while staying level shifts how powerful the subject looks. Rising above feels superior; sinking below makes them grow in stature.
A pan follows attention, like turning your head. It connects two things in the same space without cutting.
Tilting up a person or building emphasises scale and importance. Tilting down can reveal what is at their feet.
A gentle arc adds energy to a static moment and slowly changes the background behind the actor.
A full circle makes a moment feel heightened: a reunion, a victory, a turning point. The world spins while the subject stays centred.
Rising above the action pulls the audience out of the moment and shows the bigger picture. Classic for openings and endings.
The subject stays the same size while the background stretches or squeezes. It feels like vertigo or shock: the world shifting under the character.
A whip blurs the frame and creates surprise or comic energy. Editors also use it to hide a cut between two shots.
Handheld feels raw and present, as if someone is really there. Use it for chaos, panic, intimacy or realism.
A tilted horizon tells the audience something is wrong: unease, madness, a world off balance.
Moving with a character makes the audience walk with them. It builds momentum and keeps us in their journey.
Combining an arc with a push tightens the energy around the character, often used for a big emotional reveal.
